lessons.title: Computing a Capital Gain: Sale Value, Cost of Acquisition and Expenses

body.text: Your taxable gain is not simply what you sold for minus what you paid. It is the sale value the law recognises, minus the costs the law lets you count. Get either side wrong and you pay tax on money you never made, or invite a notice.

children.text: Arjun, a 34-year-old chartered accountant in Kolkata, knows the rules for his clients but still made a classic mistake on his own return. He deducted securities transaction tax from his share gains. The Income Tax Department's systems flagged the mismatch against his broker's reported figures. This lesson shows exactly what goes on each side of the calculation, so that does not happen to you.
The One Formula Behind Every Asset Class
Section 72 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (section 48 of the 1961 Act) sets out how every capital gain is computed, whether the asset is a share, a flat or a gold coin.

body.latex: \text{Capital Gain} = \text{Full Value of Consideration} - \big(\text{Transfer Expenses} + \text{Cost of Acquisition} + \text{Cost of Improvement}\big)
body.caption: If the result is negative, you have a capital loss, which Chapter 5 shows you how to set off and carry forward.

cells: The total sale value received or receivable, before any deductions
Sale price of shares, redemption value of mutual fund units, agreed price of a flat
Costs incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with the sale
Brokerage on sale, exchange and DP charges on sale, property broker commission, legal fees for the sale deed
What it cost you to acquire the asset, including incidental purchase costs
Purchase price plus brokerage, stamp duty and registration on purchase
Capital expenditure that adds to or alters the asset
Adding a floor or room to a house, building a compound wall on a plot

children.text: Side 1: The Sale Value

markDefs.definition: The entire sale consideration received or accruing on transfer of a capital asset, before deducting TDS, brokerage or any other amount. For land and buildings, it can be replaced by the stamp duty value in certain cases.

children.text: The starting point is the
full value of consideration

. Two points catch people out. First, it is the full agreed value, not the amount that lands in your bank. If a buyer deducts 1% TDS on an ₹80 lakh flat and pays you ₹79.2 lakh, your sale value is still ₹80 lakh. The ₹80,000 TDS is credited against your tax later. Second, for land and buildings, the law may substitute a higher value.
The Stamp Duty Value Rule for Property

Under section 78 of the 2025 Act (section 50C of the 1961 Act), if you sell land or a building for less than its stamp duty value, the stamp duty value is treated as your sale value. There is a safe harbour: if the stamp duty value is not more than 110% of the actual price, your actual price is accepted.

body.title: Which Sale Value Counts?
body.prompt: Nikhil sells a flat in Indore for ₹90,00,000. The stamp duty value of the flat, as assessed by the state registration authority, is ₹1,02,00,000. What is the full value of consideration for computing his capital gain?
body.explanation: 110% of the actual price is ₹99,00,000. The stamp duty value of ₹1,02,00,000 is higher than that, so the safe harbour does not apply and ₹1,02,00,000 is deemed to be the sale value, even though Nikhil only received ₹90,00,000.

body.title: What If the Stamp Duty Value Is Only Slightly Higher?

children.text: Suppose Nikhil's flat had a stamp duty value of ₹97,00,000 instead. 110% of his price is ₹99,00,000. Since ₹97,00,000 does not exceed that, his actual price of ₹90,00,000 is accepted as the sale value.

If you believe the stamp duty value is higher than the real market value of the property, you can ask the Assessing Officer to refer the valuation to a Valuation Officer. This is common for properties with legal disputes, poor access or structural issues that the circle rate does not reflect.

content.text: Where the agreement to sell fixes the price and at least part of the payment is received by account payee cheque, bank draft or electronic bank transfer on or before the date of that agreement, the stamp duty value on the agreement date can be used instead of the value on the registration date. This helps when circle rates rise between signing and registration.

children.text: Side 2: Cost of Acquisition

Cost of acquisition is the price you paid plus the incidental costs of buying. For a flat, that includes stamp duty, registration charges and legal fees on purchase. For shares bought through Zerodha, Groww or Upstox, it includes brokerage, exchange transaction charges, SEBI turnover fees, stamp duty and GST on those charges. What it does not include is securities transaction tax.

body.label: Securities Transaction Tax (STT)
body.context: Section 72 expressly bars STT from being deducted in computing capital gains, on both the buy side and the sell side. Every other normal trading charge on a delivery trade can be counted.

children.text: Had Arjun also deducted the ₹1,370 of STT, he would have reported ₹88,460. The difference is small, but the mismatch is exactly the kind of thing automated checks pick up.

body.title: Spot the Disallowed Deduction
body.question: Which of these CANNOT be deducted while computing a capital gain?
options: Brokerage paid on the sale of shares
Securities transaction tax paid on the sale of shares
Stamp duty and registration charges paid when buying a flat
The cost of adding an extra room to a house before selling it
body.explanation: STT is specifically barred by section 72 of the 2025 Act (section 48 of the 1961 Act). Sale brokerage is a transfer expense, purchase stamp duty and registration are part of the cost of acquisition, and adding a room is a cost of improvement.

children.text: When Cost Is Not What You Paid
For some assets, the law tells you what cost to use instead of an actual purchase price.

body.caption: Special cost rules you will meet in this course

cells: The previous owner's cost, under section 73 of the 2025 Act (section 49 of the 1961 Act)
Option to use fair market value on 1 April 2001. For land and buildings, that value cannot exceed the stamp duty value on that date
Bonus shares or bonus units allotted after 1 April 2001
Listed equity shares or equity fund units bought before 1 February 2018
Higher of actual cost and 31 January 2018 value, capped at sale value (grandfathering)
Fair market value on the exercise date that was taxed as salary perquisite

body.title: The Bonus Share Cost
body.textWithBlank: The cost of acquisition of bonus shares allotted to you after 1 April 2001 is taken as ___.
body.explanation: You paid nothing for bonus shares, so their cost is nil and the whole sale value is a gain. The original shares keep their full cost, so the price drop on the original shares after the bonus often creates a matching capital loss if they are sold. Chapter 2 walks through this.

children.text: Cost of Improvement

Cost of improvement is capital expenditure that adds to or changes the asset, such as building an extra room, adding a floor or constructing a compound wall on a plot. Routine repairs, painting, society maintenance and property tax are not improvements. For assets acquired before 1 April 2001, only improvement spent on or after that date counts. Shares and mutual fund units have no cost of improvement.

columns.label: Counts in the Calculation
points: Brokerage, exchange charges, SEBI fee, stamp duty and GST on share trades
Stamp duty, registration and legal fees on buying property
Broker commission and legal fees on selling property
Structural additions like an extra room, a new floor or a compound wall
The previous owner's cost for gifted or inherited assets

columns.label: Does Not Count
points: Securities transaction tax on either side of a trade
Home loan interest already claimed as a deduction under house property
Routine repairs, repainting, society maintenance and property tax
TDS deducted by the buyer, which is a tax credit, not an expense

body.title: Kavya's Plot in Ahmedabad
body.scenario: Kavya bought a residential plot on the outskirts of Ahmedabad in 2019 for ₹30,00,000 and paid ₹1,77,000 as stamp duty and registration. In 2021 she spent ₹2,00,000 building a compound wall and a borewell. In August 2026 she sells the plot for ₹58,00,000, pays her property broker 1% commission, and the buyer deducts 1% TDS and pays her the balance. The stamp duty value is ₹55,00,000.
body.prompt: Work out Kavya's capital gain. Does the stamp duty value rule apply, and should the TDS reduce her sale value?
body.modelAnswer: The stamp duty value of ₹55,00,000 is below her actual price, so section 78 does not apply and her sale value is ₹58,00,000. The buyer's TDS of ₹58,000 does not reduce the sale value. It is a tax credit she will claim in her return. Transfer expense is the 1% broker commission of ₹58,000. Cost of acquisition is ₹30,00,000 plus ₹1,77,000 = ₹31,77,000. Cost of improvement is ₹2,00,000. Capital gain = ₹58,00,000 − ₹58,000 − ₹31,77,000 − ₹2,00,000 = ₹23,65,000. She held the plot for more than 24 months, so this is a long-term gain. Because she is a resident individual who bought land before 23 July 2024, she can choose between 12.5% without indexation and 20% with indexation, which Chapter 4 covers.

children.text: Gifted and Inherited Assets

Lesson 1 showed that gifts and inheritance are not transfers. When the new owner eventually sells, section 73 treats the cost as the previous owner's cost, plus any improvement made by the previous owner or by you. If the previous owner also received it as a gift or inheritance, you keep going back until you reach the last person who actually bought it. If that purchase happened before 1 April 2001, the 1 April 2001 fair market value option is available.

body.text: The biggest real-world problem here is paperwork, not law. Families often cannot find the original sale deed or share certificates for an inherited asset. Without proof of the previous owner's cost, you risk your cost being taken as nil. Collect purchase records, old contract notes and valuation reports as soon as an asset is inherited.

body.label: Download Your Tax P&L From Zerodha Console
body.description: Most brokers provide a tax P&L that separates STT from other charges and shows buy and sell values lot by lot. Groww and Upstox offer similar reports in their tax sections.

cards.definition: Total sale value received or receivable, before TDS or brokerage. Can be replaced by stamp duty value for property.
Costs incurred wholly and exclusively for the sale, such as sale brokerage and legal fees.
Purchase price plus incidental purchase costs like brokerage, stamp duty and registration.
Capital expenditure that adds to or alters the asset, like an extra room. Not routine repairs.
Section 78, 2025 Act (old 50C): stamp duty value replaces a lower sale price for property unless it is within 110% of that price.
Securities transaction tax. Never deductible while computing capital gains.

body.title: Records to Keep for Every Asset You Own
steps: Contract notes or broker tax P&L for every share and ETF purchase
Consolidated account statement from CAMS or KFintech showing purchase NAV and date for each fund lot
Sale deed, stamp duty and registration receipts, and legal fee invoices for property
Bills and bank payment proof for any construction or structural improvement
Previous owner's purchase documents for anything gifted or inherited, plus a will or succession certificate
A registered valuer's report on 1 April 2001 value for any asset acquired before that date

points: Capital gain = full value of consideration minus transfer expenses, cost of acquisition and cost of improvement
Sale value is the full agreed amount before TDS, and for property it can be replaced by stamp duty value beyond the 110% safe harbour
Incidental purchase costs add to cost, and sale-related costs are deductible, but STT is never deductible
Cost of improvement means capital additions, not repairs, maintenance or property tax
Gifted and inherited assets use the previous owner's cost, and pre-2001 assets can use 1 April 2001 fair market value
Good records are what make these rules work in your favour
